The petitioners in these cases have called in question proceedings in Special C.C.Nos.522 of 2018,
418 of 2018 and 704 of 2020 all arising out of Crime No.4 of 2011 registered for offences punishable under Sections 120B, 409, 465, 468, 477 of the IPC r/w Section 13(1)(c) and (d) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
Since the issue in all these cases being similar, these matters are taken up together and considered by this common order.

2. Brief facts that lead the petitioners to this Court in these petitions, as borne out from respective pleadings, are as follows:-
Writ Petition No. 15106 of 2022:
The petitioner is a retired Executive Engineer, retired from the services of the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike ('the BBMP' for short) on attaining the age of superannuation.
During his tenure, the petitioner was in-charge of execution of certain works during the years 2008 to 2011.
Complaints galore on the way the works were executed by several officers of BBMP.
The work related to asphalting of new BEL Road, Ward No.5 of Malleshwaram Sub- Division.
Based on the said allegations, a crime comes to be registered against the petitioner in Crime No.4 of 2011 arraigning the petitioner as accused No.1 along with several other officers.

The matter was then entrusted to the Crime Investigation Department ('CID') for conduct of Sri B G Prakash Kumar vs State By Deputy Superintendent Of ... on 21 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/18656946/

sentences.text: The CID after investigation filed a charge sheet before the concerned Court in the year 2018 and the matter is now pending in Special C.C. No.522 of 2018.
The development in the interregnum is that the petitioner retires from service on attaining the age of superannuation.

The allegation against the petitioner is, as observed hereinabove, concerning asphalting work in the tenure of him being the Executive Engineer of Malleshwaram Sub-Division from 28-11-2008 to 21-08-2014, but the works alleged were concerning between 2008 and 2011.
Challenging filing of charge sheet and cognizance being taken by the concerned Court, the petitioner is before this Court in the subject petition.

Writ Petition No.15262 of 2022:
3.
The 1st petitioner, at the relevant point in time, was working as Engineer-in-Chief in the BBMP.
The 2nd petitioner was an employee of the State Accounts Department and was on deputation to the BBMP to the cadre of Deputy Controller.
The facts that led to registration of the crime against these petitioners are similar to what are narrated in the first of the writ petition (supra).
The allegations pertain to the very same work of asphalting against officers at different levels.
The petitioners in the subject petition are accused 5 and 6 in Crime No.4 of 2011 registered on 04-11-2011.
The CID after investigation in this case as well has filed the charge sheet and the matter is pending in Special C.C.No.418 of 2018.
In the interregnum both the petitioners have retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation.
The 1st petitioner retires on 31-05-2013 in the cadre of Engineer-in-Chief and the 2nd petitioner retires in the cadre of Deputy Controller on 30.11.2014.
Therefore, the petitioners retired before cognizance was taken by the Special Court and special criminal case being registered.
It is the registration of criminal case that is called in question in the subject petition.

Writ Petition No.17814 of 2022:
4.
The petitioners are four in number and they are accused Nos. 1, 2, 5 and 6 in the criminal case.

The 1st petitioner at the relevant point in time was working as Executive Engineer in Malleshwaram Sub-Division; the 2nd petitioner was his Assistant Executive Engineer; the 3rd petitioner was working as Chief Engineer at BBMP (West); and the 4th petitioner belonged to the State Accounts Department and was working as Deputy Controller.
The facts that led to registration of crime, the investigation and filing of the charge sheet are all similar to what is narrated as facts in the aforesaid petitions.
The proceedings are now pending against these petitioners in Special C.C.No.704 of 2020.
In the interregnum all these petitioners retired from service.
The 1st petitioner as observed hereinabove retired on 30-07-2016; the 2nd petitioner on 31-12-2015; the 3rd petitioner on 31-05-2013 and the 4th petitioner on 30-11-2014.

5. One stream that runs through all these cases is that all the petitioners in the cases at hand are all persons who have retired on attaining the age of superannuation prior to filing of the charge sheet in all the cases.
The crime that led to investigation is common in all these cases i.e., Crime No.4 of 2011.

The charge sheets filed are different, the petitioners herein are different accused in different charge sheets and have raised two common contentions in all these cases which led this Court to take them and consider together.

Heard Sri Vijaya Kumar, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, Smt. K.P.Yashodha,
learned High Court Government Pleader appearing for respondent No.1, Sri Ramu Sreekantaiah,
learned counsel appearing for respondents 2 and 3 in Writ Petition No.15106 of 2022 and Sri K.S.Mallikarjun Reddy, learned counsel appearing for respondents 2 and 3 in Writ Petition No.15262 of 2022.
7.

The learned counsel appearing for the petitioners in all these cases would vehemently contend that the allegation against the petitioners itself is erroneous and all necessary permissions and approvals were taken when asphalting work took place in the Sub- Division where most illegality is alleged.

On the legality of the conduct of proceedings, the learned counsel would submit that to proceed against the petitioners, notwithstanding they having retired from service, sanction for such prosecution was imperative which admittedly has not been obtained from the Competent Authority as obtaining under Section 197 of the CrPC and therefore, any proceeding before the concerned Court is contrary to law.

He would further contend that the very initiation of proceedings i.e.,
registration of crime and cognizance being taken runs counter to the Karnataka Civil Services Rules ('KCSRs' for short) with particular reference to sub-Rules (2), (3) & (6) of Rule 214.
It is his submission that on both these counts, the impugned proceedings are unsustainable.

8. On the other hand, the learned High Court Government Pleader representing the State would vehemently contend that sanction for offences so alleged against the petitioners is not required on two counts - one being that the offences are one of forgery and cheating as obtaining under Sections 409, 465, 468 and 477 of the IPC r/w Section 13(1)(c) and (d) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and the other being that judicial proceeding had already commenced when the crime was registered against the petitioners.
Therefore, the jurisdictional issue that the petitioners seek to project is unavailable to them.

On merits of the matter, the learned High Court Government Pleader would seek to contend that huge misappropriation of funds was committed by these petitioners to the tune of several crores as without forming the road bills were raised.
Now that the charge sheet is filed, it is a matter of trial for the petitioners to come out clean.
She would seek dismissal of the petitions.
9. The learned counsel for the BBMP-complainant would seek to toe the lines of the learned High Court Government Pleader.
10. I have given my anxious consideration to the submissions made by the respective learned counsel and have perused the material on record.
11. The afore-narrated facts are not in dispute and they lie in a narrow compass.

The submission on merits of the matter as projected by the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners is not even necessary to be noticed, as on the facts of the matter if the submission is to be accepted, it would run counter to the settled principle of law and when there are seriously disputed questions of fact the Court exercising its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC would not interfere and obliterate such proceedings for which a trial would become imperative as held by the Apex Court in the case of KAPTAN SINGH v. STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH1.

The learned counsel for the petitioners has relied on Rule 214 of the KCSRs to contend that initiation of proceedings is contrary to Rule 214(3) and (6) of the KCSRs.
Therefore it is germane to notice the said Rule.

Rule 214 (3) and (6) read as follows:
"214. ... ... ...

(3) No judicial proceedings, if not instituted while the Government servant was in service, whether before his retirement or during his re-employment, shall be instituted in respect of a cause of action which arose or in respect of an event which took place, more than four years before such institution.

(6) For the purpose of this rule,-
 (a) departmental proceedings shall be deemed to be instituted on the date on which the statement of charges is issued to the Government servant or pensioner, or if the Government servant has been placed under suspension from an earlier date, on such date: and (b) judicial proceedings shall be deemed to be instituted-  (i) in the case of criminal proceedings, on the date  on which the complaint or report of a police  officer, of which the Magistrate takes  cognizance is made; and (ii) in the case of civil proceedings, on the date the plaint is presented in the court."

Rule 214(3) mandates that no judicial proceeding if not instituted while the Government servant was in service, whether before his retirement or during his re-employment, shall be instituted in respect of a cause of action which arose or in respect of an event which took place, more than four years before such institution.
Sub- rule (6) defines what is judicial proceeding.

Judicial proceedings shall be deemed to be instituted in case of criminal proceedings on the date the complaint or report of a police officer, of which the Magistrate takes cognizance of such report and in the case of civil proceedings, the date of plaint presented before the Court.

13. The learned counsel submits that criminal proceedings though were registered on 04-11-2011 in Crime No.4 of 2011, investigation took seven years to complete and the charge sheets are filed between the years 2018 and 2020 and by then the petitioners in these cases had retired and,
therefore, the very taking of cognizance is erroneous.
This submission is unacceptable.

The definition is clear that in case of criminal proceedings judicial proceedings shall be deemed to be Sri B G Prakash Kumar vs State By Deputy Superintendent Of ... on 21 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/18656946/
8 instituted on the date on which the complaint or a report of the Police officer, of which the Magistrate takes cognizance.

Therefore, the submission of the learned counsel for the petitioners qua Rule 214 of the KCSRs tumbles down and is rejected.
14. The other submission is with regard to obtaining of sanction from the hands of the Competent Authority to continue trial, for which it is necessary to notice Section 197 of the CrPC.
The allegations against the petitioners are offences under the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Since the petitioners have retired from service what would become applicable or otherwise is Section 197 of the CrPC and not Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

Therefore, it is germane to notice Section 197 of the CrPC and it runs as follows:
"197. Prosecution of Judges and public servants.--(1) When any person who is or was a Judge or Magistrate or a public servant not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government is accused of any offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, no Court shall take cognizance of such offence except with the previous sanction save as otherwise provided in the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (1 of 2014)--
(a) in the case of a person who is employed or, as the case may be, was at the time of commission of the alleged offence employed, in connection with the affairs of the Union, of the Central Government;
(b) in the case of a person who is employed or, as the case may be, was at the time of commission of the alleged offence employed, in connection with the affairs of a State,
of the State Government:
Provided that where the alleged offence was committed by a person referred to in clause (b) during the period while a Proclamation issued under clause (1) of article 356 of the Constitution was in force in a State, clause (b) will apply as if for the expression "State Government" occurring therein, the expression "Central Government" were substituted.
Explanation.--For the removal of doubts it is hereby declared that no sanction shall be required in case of a public servant accused of any offence alleged to have been committed under section 166A, section 166B, section 354, section 354A, section 354B, section 354C, section 354D, section 370, section 375, section 376, section 376A, section 376C, section 376D or section 509 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860)."
Any act of public servant in the course of discharge of his official duty is alleged to become an ingredient of offence under any penal law, sanction for such prosecution is imperative.

sentences.text:
The Special Judge framed charges on 7-6-2005 against all seven accused for the offences under Sections 218/409/465/467/120-B IPC and under Section 13(1)(c)
read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 ("the PC Act", for short).

Out of six charges framed, one pertained to the offence under Section 13(1)(c)
read with Section 13(2) of the PC Act while other five related to the offences under the Penal Code, 1860.
6. The public servants, namely, Sikandar Singh and Labh Singh challenged the aforesaid order dated 7-6-2005 by filing Criminal Revision No. 1743 of 2005 in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana.

entities.text: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The High Court took the view that the department had refused sanction to prosecute public servants and yet a challan was presented on the premise that no sanction was required after retirement of those public servants.

The High Court observed:
"These petitioners and others have been charged for offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act and also for the offences under the Penal Code.
Section 197 CrPC bars cognizance by the Court of an offence by a public servant even after retirement.

Even otherwise, it is discriminatory for the petitioners when other co-accused who are still in service, cannot be prosecuted for want of sanction and present petitioners are being prosecuted only because they have retired."
The High Court allowed the petition and set aside the order dated 7-6-2005 passed by the Special Judge, Patiala.
7.
This appeal by the State of Punjab takes exception to the order of the High Court.

During the pendency of this appeal the first respondent Sikandar Singh expired and his name was deleted from the array of parties vide order dated 20-9-2010 passed by this (2014)16 SCC 807 Court, leaving Labh Singh as the only respondent before the Court.

The stand taken in the petition of appeal on behalf of the appellant is as under:
"It is humbly submitted that order passed by the Hon'ble High Court is erroneous in law as under Section 197 CrPC the respondents can be convicted and no previous sanction is required as the respondents are no longer in service and have been retired in the years 1999/2000.
Secondly, there was no discrimination as the other persons were in service and since the respondents have been retired no previous sanction is required.
It was also submitted that other persons will also be prosecuted as and when they are retired."

10 8. Appearing for the State Mr Sanchar Anand, learned Advocate submitted that sanction to prosecute was not required at all.
Ms Jaspreet Gogia, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent supported the view taken by the High Court.
9. In the present case the public servants in question had retired on 13-12-1999 and 30-4-2000.
The sanction to prosecute them was rejected subsequent to their retirement i.e. first on 13-9-2000 and later on 24-9-2003.
The public servants having retired from service there was no occasion to consider grant of sanction under Section 19 of the PC Act.

The law on the point is quite clear that sanction to prosecute the public servant for the offences under the PC Act is not required if the public servant had already retired on the date of cognizance by the court.

In S.A. Venkataraman v.
State [S.A. Venkataraman v. State, AIR 1958 SC 107 : 1958 Cri LJ 254 : 1958 SCR 1040] while construing Section 6(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 which provision is in pari materia with Section 19(1) of the PC Act, this Court held that no sanction was necessary in the case of a person who had ceased to be the public servant at the time the court was asked to take cognizance.

sentences.text: 10. However as regards charges for the offences punishable under the Penal Code, the High Court was absolutely right in setting aside the order of the Special Judge.

Unlike Section 19 of the PC Act,
the protection under Section 197 CrPC is available to the public servant concerned even after retirement.

Therefore, if the matter was considered by the sanctioning authority and the sanction to prosecute was rejected first on 13-9-2000 and secondly on 24-9-2003, the Court could not have taken cognizance insofar as the offences punishable under the Penal Code are concerned.

As laid down by this Court in State of H.P. v. Nishant Sareen [State of H.P. v. Nishant Sareen, (2010) 14 SCC 527 : (2011) 3 SCC (Cri) 836] , the recourse in such cases is either to challenge the order of the sanctioning authority or to approach it again if there is any fresh material.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
On the legality of the conduct of proceedings, the learned counsel would submit that to proceed against the petitioners, notwithstanding they having retired from service, sanction for such prosecution was imperative which admittedly has not been obtained from the Competent Authority as obtaining under Section 197 of the CrPC and therefore, any proceeding before the concerned Court is contrary to law.
8. On the other hand, the learned High Court Government Pleader representing the State would vehemently contend that sanction for offences so alleged against the petitioners is not required on two counts - one being that the offences are one of forgery and cheating as obtaining under Sections 409, 465, 468 and 477 of the IPC r/w Section 13(1)(c) and (d) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and the other being that judicial proceeding had already commenced when the crime was registered against the petitioners.
Therefore, the petitioners cannot contend that cognizance is taken by the learned Magistrate in the year 2018 and, therefore, is barred by Rule 214(3) & (6) of the KCSRs supra.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The allegations against the petitioners are offences under the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Since the petitioners have retired from service what would become applicable or otherwise is Section 197 of the CrPC and not Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
9. In the present case the public servants in question had retired on 13-12-1999 and 30-4-2000.
The sanction to prosecute them was rejected subsequent to their retirement i.e. first on 13-9-2000 and later on 24-9-2003.
The public servants having retired from service there was no occasion to consider grant of sanction under Section 19 of the PC Act.
The law on the point is quite clear that sanction to prosecute the public servant for the offences under the PC Act is not required if the public servant had already retired on the date of cognizance by the court.
In S.A. Venkataraman v.
State [S.A. Venkataraman v. State, AIR 1958 SC 107 : 1958 Cri LJ 254 : 1958 SCR 1040] while construing Section 6(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 which provision is in pari materia with Section 19(1) of the PC Act, this Court held that no sanction was necessary in the case of a person who had ceased to be the public servant at the time the court was asked to take cognizance.
The view taken in S.A. Venkataraman [S.A. Venkataraman v. State, AIR 1958 SC 107 : 1958 Cri LJ 254 :
1958 SCR 1040] was adopted by this Court in C.R. Bansi v. State of Maharashtra [C.R. Bansi v. State of Maharashtra, (1970) 3 SCC 537 : 1971 SCC (Cri) 143] and in Kalicharan Mahapatra v. State of Orissa [Kalicharan Mahapatra v. State of Orissa,
(1998) 6 SCC 411 : 1998 SCC (Cri) 1455] and by the Constitution Bench of this Court in K. Veeraswami v. Union of India [K. Veeraswami v. Union of India, (1991) 3 SCC 655 : 1991 SCC (Cri) 734] . The High Court was not therefore justified in setting aside the order passed by the Special Judge insofar as charge under the PC Act was concerned.
10. However as regards charges for the offences punishable under the Penal Code, the High Court was absolutely right in setting aside the order of the Special Judge.
Unlike Section 19 of the PC Act,
the protection under Section 197 CrPC is available to the public servant concerned even after retirement.
Therefore, if the matter was considered by the sanctioning authority and the sanction to prosecute was rejected first on 13-9-2000 and secondly on 24-9-2003, the Court could not have taken cognizance insofar as the offences punishable under the Penal Code are concerned.
As laid down by this Court in State of H.P. v. Nishant Sareen [State of H.P. v. Nishant Sareen, (2010) 14 SCC 527 : (2011) 3 SCC (Cri) 836] , the recourse in such cases is either to challenge the order of the sanctioning authority or to approach it again if there is any fresh material.
11. In the circumstances, in our view the order under appeal passed by the High Court is correct insofar as charges under IPC are concerned but must be set aside as regards charge under the PC Act is concerned.
The Apex Court was considering the issue whether once the public servant would retire, sanction for prosecution would be necessary or otherwise, notwithstanding the fact that the allegations leveled against those public servants are the ones in discharge of their official duties while they were in service.
The Apex Court has clearly answered that, sanction for such prosecution even against retired persons is necessary.
In the light of the issue standing covered by the judgment of the Apex Court and the admitted fact, that sanction is not even sought from the hands of the Competent Authority to be placed before the concerned Court for continuing the trial,
further proceedings before the concerned Court cannot be permitted to continue unless the prosecution obtains and places before the concerned Court a valid sanction from the Competent Authority.
